1.pericope_label: It is not expedient for me doubtless to glory. I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven. And I knew such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.

schools.summary: Note that the opening sentence is textually unsettled, and judge the best-attested text to be one running in English as I must needs glory; it is not, indeed, expedient, but I will come — reading the sequence of thought as mingled feelings, the writer constrained by his opponents' taunts into what looked like self-assertion while conscious it was not in the highest sense expedient. Explain the third person as forced by the charge of boasting, since although he could not boast directly he could tell of a man about whom there would be no impropriety in boasting; and note that speaking of oneself so is not uncommon, instancing Caesar's practice and the fourth evangelist's way of referring to himself. Reckon back from a letter of about the year fifty-seven to arrive at forty-three, placing the vision in the unrecorded activity before the arrival at Antioch where such an encouragement would have been unspeakably precious, and set aside the trance in the temple. Then take the two raptures: the stress laid on the second hinders us from thinking it identical with the first, and the nearest distinction possible is that the one revealed the glory of the throne as Moses and Isaiah and Ezekiel saw it while the other brought before the spirit the peace ineffable — or, on the other view, hold that paradise is apparently used as the equivalent of the third heaven, note that some Jewish writers place paradise there while the rabbis reckoned two heavens, three, or seven, and caution against committing the apostle to any celestial gradation. On the word itself, trace it from eastern Asia into Greek and the western languages, giving the Sanskrit sense of a cultivated upland, the Armenian of a garden about a house, and the Persian of the walled pleasure-parks of princes.

Ask why it should be inexpedient to glory at all, since a man knows his own revelations whether he speaks of them or not, and answer that knowing them ourselves does not lift us up so much as publishing them to others, since it is not the nature of good deeds to exalt a man but their being witnessed to and known. Distinguish the two kinds of boasting in view: the great grounds were those already recounted, the trials, but there are other things also to tell of, the revelations and the unspeakable mysteries — and it is of these that he says it is not expedient, meaning lest they lift him up to pride.

Read the restraint as a rebuke of the rivals, since it was a shame that they should scrape commendations together from every quarter to put themselves on a level with so distinguished a man; and warn that the more numerous a man's graces the less he ought to think of his own excellence, such a thought being a labyrinth in which one is dazzled while remaining ignorant of himself. Then give the reason for the third person in the writer's own voice: I should have preferred to be silent and keep the whole matter suppressed, but these obstinate persons will not allow me, and so I shall mention it as it were in a stammering way, that it may be seen I speak through constraint. Take the confession of not knowing whether he was in the body or out of it as expressing the greatness of the revelation rather than any uncertainty of mind.

Report that there are several readings of the opening verse, too minute to set out, whose effect is that if it be expedient to glory, which does not become him, he will proceed to visions. On the dating, reckon fourteen years back from a letter of about fifty-seven to the year forty-two or forty-three, and place the vision near the journey from Tarsus to Antioch or the errand to Jerusalem with alms, noting that it was kept secret for fourteen years. Then hold that the third heaven and paradise are probably not the same place, so that there were likely at least two raptures; report that the Jewish writers have four paradises as they have seven heavens, and that among Christian writers the word generally means the place of the blessed or the state of separate spirits. On the unspeakable words, recall that the Jews held the divine name unlawful to utter and say the true pronunciation is lost.

debates.question: Is one rapture described, or two?

sides.position: Two: the third heaven and paradise are probably not the same place
Two: the stress laid on the second hinders us from thinking it identical with the first in time or subject
One: paradise is apparently used as the equivalent of the third heaven, and we should not commit the apostle to any celestial gradation

debates.question: Why is the account given in the third person?

sides.position: Because he had been accused of boasting, and could tell of a man about whom boasting would be no impropriety
To show that he speaks through constraint, mentioning it as it were in a stammering way
Through modesty, since the account can be understood of no one else

debates.question: Why is it not expedient to glory?

sides.position: Lest it lift him up to pride; knowing our own good deeds does not exalt us so much as publishing them
Because the more numerous a man's graces the less he should think of his own excellence

outliers.note: Alone works the philology of the surrounding language rather than the theology, and alone canvasses and dismisses the trance in the temple as the occasion of the vision before settling on the unrecorded years before Antioch.
Alone asks why publishing a revelation should be more dangerous than having one, and answers that it is not the nature of good deeds to exalt a man but their being witnessed to and known by others.

themes: visions and revelations of the Lord
caught up to the third heaven
unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter

5.pericope_label: Of such an one will I glory: yet of myself I will not glory, but in mine infirmities. For though I would desire to glory, I shall not be a fool; for I will say the truth: but now I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth me to be, or that he heareth of me.

schools.summary: Report both readings of the phrase before choosing. Some take the words to mean of such a thing or such a transaction, so that the writer may boast of being caught up as of an event whose whole glory belongs to the one who exalted him, while of himself he will not boast; name the two who explain it so and reject them, since the connexion requires a person and the passage is partly ironical, the writer keeping himself out of view and saying only that of such a man they would admit it proper to boast. Then turn the division of the self into a meditation: there is an almost exquisite sadness in the distinction between the old self of fourteen years ago with its abundance of revelations and the new self of the present, feebler and sadder, worn with cares and the daily rush of life; then he saw with open vision, now he walks by faith and can hardly recognise his own identity, speaking of the man who once had that capacity as though he were another and almost as if he were dead and gone. Generalise the experience and then withdraw the generalisation — the soldier recalling the rush of battle, the poet finding the faculty divine no longer entrusted to him, the orator who once wielded a fierce democracy complaining of a stammering tongue — but this case has a sadness peculiar to itself, since faith and hope and love remain while a glory has passed from the earth. On the disclaimer, take the sentence as serious rather than ironical: if he chose to boast as others did he would have ample material and would not be boasting emptily.

Describe the manoeuvre as a distinguishing of himself from himself, himself in paradise from himself on earth, so that though he might lawfully glory of a person so exalted he chose to forbear because the case was his own.

Say bluntly that modesty alone prevents the naming, since the account can be understood of no one else and would otherwise be wholly irrelevant. Then draw the practical moral out of the abrupt breaking-off: ask who that had received such honour would have kept silence about it for fourteen years, and observe that the revelations were mentioned for two opposite reasons, lest enemies think meanly of him and, having said that much, lest friends think too highly — for it is a rare gift to discern when to speak and when to be silent, and to know when enough is said, neither too little nor too much.

debates.question: Does of such an one mean a person or a thing?

sides.position: A thing, or such a transaction — the glory of it belonging wholly to the one who exalted him
A person: the connexion requires it, and the passage is partly ironical
A person — himself, distinguished from himself, himself in paradise from himself on earth

debates.question: What is the tone of the distinction between the two selves?

sides.position: An almost exquisite sadness: he can hardly recognise his own identity and speaks of his former self as though dead and gone
As if there were two Pauls — and in a sense there were

debates.question: Is the disclaimer that follows ironical or serious?

sides.position: Serious: if he chose to boast as others do he would have ample material and would not be boasting emptily
Serious, but keyed to the vocabulary of madness dominant in the words for fool and folly

outliers.note: Alone turns the grammatical division between the old self and the new into an extended meditation on the loss of visionary power with age, ranging over the soldier, the poet and the orator before saying that this case has a sadness peculiar to itself.

Alone draws a practical rule from the fourteen years of silence, that it is a rare gift to discern when to speak and when to be silent, and to know when enough is said, neither too little nor too much.

themes: of such an one will I glory, yet of myself I will not glory
I shall not be a fool, for I will say the truth
lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth me to be

7.pericope_label: And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.

schools.summary: Begin with the word rather than the conjectures. The Greek would better be rendered stake: it is used of the stakes driven in to form a palisade round a grave, as in the Iliad where they dig a trench full deep and fix their stakes about it, and a sharp-pointed stake of that kind was the instrument of impaling, the Greek verbs for impaling and crucifying being almost interchangeable, so that Euripides can ask whether to hurl the captives from a rock or fix their bodies on the stake — and opponents of the faith like Celsus and Lucian preferred the word stake to cross as more ignominious, speaking of Jesus as having been impaled. Leave the identification aside and dwell on the stated purpose, arguing that the man was naturally proud, self-confident and eminently ambitious, so that pride would be his besetting sin after conversion and no one else should be surprised to need such a measure. Argue from the following verse that the prayer was addressed to Christ, noting that even Rosenmuller maintained it and the Socinians themselves admit it, and drawing the conclusion that it is right to go to Christ in trouble and right to worship him. Hear behind the threefold prayer the threefold prayer in Gethsemane, where likewise the answer was not compliance but strength to endure. Report that some of the better manuscripts omit the possessive in the reply, so that it becomes a general axiom that might is perfected in weakness, and regret that the received rendering conceals the identity of that word with the one translated infirmity just after; note too that the verb is linear, so power is continually increased as the weakness grows.

Define the thorn broadly and by a distinction: under the term is comprehended every kind of temptation with which the apostle was exercised, and flesh here denotes not the body but that part of the soul which has not yet been regenerated. Be emphatic in rejecting one reading in particular, that those act a ridiculous part who think the temptation was to lust, a fancy which must be repudiated and put far away. Report the headache view without endorsing it, and say that Chrysostom inclined rather to refer the thorn to Hymeneus and Alexander and men like them, who under the devil's instigation gave much annoyance. On the answer, hold it not certain and not greatly important whether it came by special revelation, since God answers us when he strengthens us inwardly by his Spirit so that we do not give up hope and patience; and take grace here to mean not the favour of God as elsewhere but the aid of the Holy Spirit which comes from that favour.

Note that the noun means a stake and the cognate verb to be tied to one by way of punishment, and that the word is used of the most oppressive afflictions; insist that whatever it was it was outward, since it was neither sin nor sinfulness, sin having never had and never being able to have the tendency to keep a man from being exalted. List the older conjectures and assign them — earache to Tertullian, headache to Chrysostom, many grievous bodily torments to Cyprian — and hold that the reference is simply to the distresses endured through the opposition at Corinth. Argue that the prayer was addressed to Christ and call it a sure proof of divinity, since only an omniscient being can be made an object of prayer; suggest that three stands either for an indefinite many or for three solemn and fixed applications, and hear an allusion to the threefold prayer in Gethsemane. Gloss the resting of the power as overshadowing like a tent, affording shelter, protection and rest.

debates.question: What was the thorn in the flesh?

sides.position: The distresses endured through the opposition at Corinth; whatever it was, it was outward and neither sin nor sinfulness
Every kind of temptation he was exercised with; flesh here means not the body but the unregenerate part of the soul — and the reading that makes it a temptation to lust must be repudiated
The older conjectures assign earache to Tertullian, headache to Chrysostom, and many grievous bodily torments to Cyprian
Chrysostom inclined rather to Hymeneus and Alexander and men like them, who under the devil's instigation gave much annoyance

debates.question: To whom was the prayer addressed?

sides.position: To Christ, as the following verse proves; even Rosenmuller maintained it and the Socinians admit it
To Christ, which is a sure proof of his divinity, since only an omniscient being can be an object of prayer
Either a certain number for an uncertain, or three solemn and fixed applications
Frequent repetition, the number standing for a large but indefinite one
Three, with the threefold prayer in Gethsemane behind it

outliers.note: Alone establishes the sense of the central word before touching the conjectures, showing from Homer, Herodotus and Euripides that it means a stake, and noting that Celsus and Lucian preferred stake to cross as the more ignominious term for the crucifixion.

Alone defines the thorn as every kind of temptation and flesh as the unregenerate part of the soul rather than the body, and alone singles out the reading that makes it a temptation to lust in order to call it a ridiculous fancy that must be put far away.

themes: a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me
my grace is sufficient for thee
when I am weak, then am I strong

11.pericope_label: I am become a fool in glorying; ye have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended of you: for in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing. Truly the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds. For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong.

schools.summary: Explain the unfulfilled obligation in the tense: he means he ought now to be commended by them instead of having to glorify himself. Hear the whole closing section as an echo of the storm just passed, since it reproduces in compressed form most of the earlier topics, each with its characteristic phrase, so that the violence is over but the sky is not yet clear and we still hear the mutterings of receding thunder — he remembers again that he has been called insane, taunted with commending himself, treated as nothing beside those rivals who set themselves up as apostles extraordinary. Report that the two words for glorying are wanting in the better manuscripts, so the verse opens with a thrilling abruptness. On the signs, note the word is used first in the general sense of tokens and then specifically of works of supernatural power, count the three separate words for miracle standing together, and mark the passage as one where the apostle distinctly claims such power for himself and appeals to its exercise. Then measure the closing verse against the orators: it contains a striking mixture of sarcasm and irony not exceeded by any example in Demosthenes, and the sting is that they are inferior to other churches in one respect only, that they were never burdened with the privilege of supporting him — for which wrong he asks their pardon. Note that the word for being burdensome is the characteristic term for sponging which his rivals had used of him.

Notice that the self-accusation has hardened as the passage went on: at the outset he asked to be received as foolish and spoke as in foolishness, but now, dropping the qualifying particle, he calls himself foolish outright; and having established his point he grapples unsparingly with the whole failing, teaching that none should praise himself where there is no necessity, since even where a reason existed this man called himself a fool for doing it. Then observe where the blame is laid — not on the false apostles but wholly on the disciples, since it was they who compelled him.

Blame them for what was faulty: they had not stood up in his defence as they ought, and so made it the more needful for him to insist on his own vindication; they in a manner compelled him to commend himself, who ought to have been commended of them. Add that they in particular had good reason to speak well of him, since he had given them full proof of his apostleship, the signs of an apostle having been wrought among them in all patience.

Mark the change of posture: having until now solicited their forgiveness by various apologies for a thing contrary to his own custom and to what was due his office, he stops soliciting and upbraids, throwing the blame on the Corinthians who ought to have been the first to praise him and to set themselves vigorously against the calumniators. Take the patience differently from the others, referring it either to his remaining invincible under every assault or, more probably, to his enduring injuries in silence and overcoming indignities by patience, since such heroic virtue is itself a kind of heavenly seal. Then turn the last verse into a charge of double ingratitude, since they had not only held in contempt the man whose kindness had put them under obligation but had turned his very generosity into an occasion of reproach — which is not merely insulting his modesty but cruelty.

debates.question: Who is to blame for the boasting?

sides.position: Wholly the disciples, not the false apostles, since it was they who compelled him
The Corinthians, who ought to have been the first to praise him and to withstand the calumniators
They ought now to be commending him instead of his having to glorify himself

debates.question: What is the patience in which the signs were wrought?

sides.position: Endurance of every kind, referring to the hardships and privations already specified
Either remaining invincible under assault, or enduring injuries in silence — such heroic virtue being itself a heavenly seal
Persevering in furnishing the evidence notwithstanding unreasonable opposition

debates.question: How sharp is the closing verse?

sides.position: A striking mixture of sarcasm and irony not exceeded by any example in Demosthenes
Consummate irony directed at the stingy element in the church
A charge of double ingratitude, since they turned his very generosity into an occasion of reproach

outliers.note: Alone tracks how the self-accusation hardens across the passage, from asking to be received as foolish to calling himself foolish outright once the qualifying particle is dropped.
Alone reads the closing section as the receding thunder of a storm already passed, in which each earlier reproach is recalled once more in compressed form.

themes: I am become a fool in glorying: ye have compelled me
the signs of an apostle were wrought among you

14.pericope_label: Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children. And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved. But be it so, I did not burden you: nevertheless, being crafty, I caught you with guile. Did I make a gain of you by any of them whom I sent unto you? I desired Titus, and with him I sent a brother. Did Titus make a gain of you? walked we not in the same spirit? walked we not in the same steps?

schools.summary: Settle how many visits are counted: he does not mean he had been with them twice already but that he had twice before formed and been disappointed of the purpose, having intended to call both on the way to Macedonia and on the return — or, counting differently, reckon the long first sojourn as the first occasion, the projected journey from Ephesus as the second, and the present preparation as the third. Note that the verb for being burdensome now appears for the third time in the letter, so they need not be apprehensive. On the spending, note that the second verb implies spending to the last farthing, so that as he sought not theirs but them he is ready to spend not only all he has but all that he is; and find the painful undertone in what follows, an intense craving for affection to which it seemed their love varied inversely with his own. Then handle the charge of craft: it cannot be a serious admission of having caught them by fraud, since the objection is answered in the next verse; reconstruct the sneer in the objectors' voice, granting that he made no demands on their purses in person but asking what to think of the collection for the saints and whose pockets it will reach, since they know him subtle enough to take them in somehow. Note that the word for crafty is quoted from the enemies, and that a modern translator has done well to put the charges in quotation marks.

Account for the obscurity of the sentence by its subject: since he was speaking about money and his defence on that score, it is reasonable that what he says be wrapped in obscurity. Then set out the objection he is meeting by anticipation — that though he took nothing himself, being crafty he procured those sent by him to ask something as for themselves, and so received through others while keeping clear of the appearance of receiving.

Give two reasons for the refusal of support, that he sought not their wealth and that he wished to act a father's part; and draw the pastoral rule while immediately guarding it, that a genuine pastor seeks not gain from his sheep but their welfare, though ministers are not to seek men with a view to having disciples of their own. Call the readiness to lay out not merely his endeavours but life itself an evidence of more than fatherly affection, and observe that he continues to cherish it while regarded with coldness — asking what heart, though hard as iron, such ardour would not soften, especially joined to such constancy. Add that this is set down not that we may admire him but that we may imitate him, and that all pastors should learn from it what they owe their churches.

Turn the fatherhood into an observation from ordinary life: it frequently happens to loving fathers that their disobedient children love them less in proportion as their own love increases, and the most disobedient child is often the one on which the parents' tenderness is especially placed, as the shepherd feels more for the lost sheep than for the ninety-nine — and it is in the order of God that it should be so, else the case of every prodigal would be utterly deplorable. Then state the stakes on the confession of craft: many suppose the phrase about catching them with guile is the apostle's own, and have concluded from it that guile and deceit are lawful in service of a religious purpose; say that this doctrine is abominable and that the words are most evidently those of his detractors, against which he defends himself in the verses following.

debates.question: How many visits are being counted?

sides.position: Two previous purposes, both disappointed; this is the third resolution, not the third visit
The long first sojourn, then the projected journey from Ephesus, then this
The phrasing suggests only one visit so far

debates.question: Whose words are being crafty, I caught you with guile?

sides.position: His detractors'; many suppose them his own and conclude guile is lawful for a religious purpose, which doctrine is abominable
The objectors'; it cannot be a serious admission of fraud, and it is answered in the next verse
The objectors', quoted from them — a modern translator has done well to put the charges in quotation marks
The objectors', extending even to a suspicion that the collection for the saints might be a trap

outliers.note: Alone names and condemns the inference some had drawn from this verse, that guile and deceit are lawful in service of a religious purpose, calling the doctrine abominable and the words plainly those of the detractors.
Alone explains the obscurity of the sentence by its subject, that where money and a defence about money are concerned it is reasonable the words should be wrapped in obscurity.

themes: I seek not yours, but you
I will very gladly spend and be spent for you
being crafty, I caught you with guile

19.pericope_label: Again, think ye that we excuse ourselves unto you? we speak before God in Christ: but we do all things, dearly beloved, for your edifying. For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults: And lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed.

schools.summary: Report that many of the best manuscripts give the word for long ago rather than the word for again, in which case the sentence is better taken as an assertion than a question: you are thinking, and have been thinking for a long time, that it is to you we have been making our defence. Note that the Greek verb is the one always used of a formal vindication, and that the writer deprecates the idea of entering on such a thing at all, being anxious to explain his conduct but refusing to acknowledge that he stands at the bar of their judgment-seat — he is not just apologising but is in deadly earnest, as they will find out when he comes. Then work the list of disorders closely, setting it against the catalogue of the fruits of repentance earlier in the letter as a suggestive parallelism of contrast, the same keen perception of the shades of human character dwelling now on the manifold forms of opposition; correct the received renderings, noting that debates should rather be strifes or quarrels and that the English word carried a darker shade in older usage. Add that the word for whisperings is onomatopoeic, imitating the sibilant murmur of a snake charmer, and that of the word for backbitings one could wish it existed nowhere else. Finally recover a connection the English loses, that the verb for humbling reproduces the word already prominent in the letter and rendered variously as cast down, base and abasing, so that there is something almost plaintive in speaking of his disciples' sin as the only real humiliation he has to fear.

Explain how a man's own vindication can serve his readers' edification: because he had been brought into contempt many grew wanton as with loosened reins, so that respect for him would have been a means of leading them to repentance, since then they would have listened to his admonitions. Add that it is a fault in Christ's servants to be too much concerned about their own reputation, which is why he declares first that he speaks in God's presence and second that he has more concern for them than for himself. Then find in the fear expressed a token not merely of love but of indulgence, since it shuns severity and reaches for milder measures: I strive now to maintain my authority so that I may not be constrained to punish your obstinacy more severely when I come. Teach by that example that mild remedies must always be tried first.

Read the verb for fearing as a present standing for a past, so that the verse explains why he had not come before and had sent Titus instead, being unwilling to use the rod — on which reading all difficulty vanishes, whereas otherwise the statement seems to contradict what was said earlier in the letter. Deny that any sinister or unworthy motive lay behind the sending, and say that whatever was done was done for their edifying and not for any advantage to himself or his friends. Then read the closing verse as a fear of humiliation in the older sense of deep affliction, and infer from the state described that there must have been a total relaxation of discipline, else such things could not have been tolerated — so that this church, a composition of excellences and defects, should not be quoted as a model.

debates.question: Does the verse open with again or long ago?

sides.position: Long ago, on many of the best manuscripts, which turns the sentence from a question into an assertion
Again — do you think we make an apology for our conduct?

debates.question: Is the fear expressed present or past?

sides.position: The present stands for the past, explaining why he had not come before and sent Titus instead
Present: the old anxiety which had led him to postpone the visit comes back on his spirit

debates.question: Why speak of his own vindication at all?

sides.position: Not to clear himself from aspersions but to edify, under a sense that God is his judge
Because contempt for him had let many grow wanton, so that respect for him would lead them to repentance

outliers.note: Alone reads the verb for fearing as a present standing for a past, and claims that on this reading an apparent contradiction with an earlier chapter of the letter vanishes.
Alone works through the vice-list word by word as a formal counterpart to the earlier catalogue of the fruits of repentance, and alone dates the English word debates by its darker older usage.

themes: we speak before God in Christ
lest there be debates, envyings, wraths
lest my God will humble me among you
